To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) the quantum theory can be given a physical interpretation in terms of hidden, or "subquantum", variables, (2) in principle, these hidden variables determine the precise outcomes of individual measurement processes, but (3) in practice, the observed system is so disturbed in measurements that we can carry out that the uncertainty principle appears as a practical limitation.

(1) the wave function does not provide an exhaustive description of a physical system at the quantum mechanical level; (2) there exist hidden variables that do provide such an exhaustive description; (3) in principle, these hidden variables determine the exact result of each individual measurement; (4) in practice, these exact results are unobservable in the present state of technology, because of the disturbance caused by the observing apparatus

the wave function is a probability amplitude for the occurrence of a particular set of values of the hidden variables, and that these values are determined at the time of measurement in a way that is consistent with the quantum theory.
